paras: The Wrightsville lynching threat was a threat by white citizens of Wrightsville, Pennsylvania, in August 1903 to lynch unidentified Black men accused of chasing white women on the town's streets at night. No one was reported caught or harmed, and the episode is known only from a single York dispatch carried by two Washington-area papers on August 15, 1903.

According to the dispatch, the Susquehanna River town was "in a state of excitement" over "unknown negroes who chase and try to seize and assault unprotected white women on the streets at night." A dozen women were said to have been "thoroughly frightened" over the previous several nights.

The Washington Times version added that on Thursday night a man pursued Lena Proff for several blocks, and that she was still suffering "severe nervous shock" the next day. Citizens were reported to be planning to apprehend the offenders and threatening, if they succeeded, "to deal out lynch law." The Alexandria Gazette added that the situation had caused "race feeling to become strong among the whites of the town."
The coverage does not report any arrest, capture or lynching, and no later report on the episode was found. None of the men accused was named or identified.

The Washington Times ran the dispatch on page 2 under the headline "Pennsylvania Women Chased by Negroes," with the deck "Citizens Threaten Lynching if Miscreants Are Apprehended." The Alexandria Gazette printed a nearly identical paragraph, without the Proff incident, in its "News of the Day" column, between an item on Black residents fleeing Whitesboro, Texas, and a train collision in West Virginia. Both papers stated the accusations as fact and reported the lynching threat without comment.
No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

framing.detail: The Alexandria Gazette ran the dispatch as one paragraph among the day's news, stating the accusations as fact and adding that race feeling was 'strong among the whites'.
The Washington Times headlined it 'Pennsylvania Women Chased by Negroes' and called the unidentified men 'Miscreants' while reporting the lynching threat without comment.
